      Abstract
Probabilistic Boolean circuits have recently been proposed as a string-diagrammatic foundation for
finite probabilistic programming. In this paper, we present a complete set of axioms for their semantics
in terms of Markov kernels. Our approach is based on two intermediate results: completeness for
partial Boolean circuits and completeness for probabilistic Boolean tapes, a diagrammatic language
for rig categories.

 1      Introduction
Diagrammatic languages play a central role in computer science, with classical examples
including Petri nets, graph rewriting systems [23, 29], and data- and control-flow diagrams [5],
among others. More recently, the increasing importance of spatial structure in computation
led Milner to move beyond the traditional term-based syntax of process calculi and introduce
bigraphs [53]. Similar trends arise in quantum computing [63, 25, 1, 20, 3, 39] and probabilistic
programming [49, 26, 62, 67, 51], where–unlike in classical computation–information cannot
be freely copied or discarded. More broadly, the shift towards viewing data as a physical
resource rather than a purely logical entity (see, e.g., [58, 37]) has driven the widespread
adoption [4, 14, 16, 30, 31, 38, 55, 61, 13, 18, 44, 60, 12, 28, 27, 45, 54, 34, 33, 36, 67, 59, 35, 32]
of string diagrams [47, 65] as a graphical syntax.
    Formally, string diagrams are morphisms in the symmetric monoidal category freely
generated by a monoidal signature Σ, which we denote by DiagΣ . The signature contains
a basic set of generating symbols and complex diagrams are built via horizontal (;) and
vertical (⊗) composition. Such diagrams are typically interpreted in a monoidal category C
via a map ⟨⟨·⟩⟩ : DiagΣ → C assigning semantics to each diagram. When ⟨⟨·⟩⟩ is a monoidal
functor–i.e., it preserves both ; and ⊗–the semantics is compositional, and the induced notion
of semantic equality forms a congruence. Axiomatizing this congruence is a central challenge,
as it enables equational reasoning directly at the level of diagrams.

    The move from circuits to tapes allows us to reason not only about the monoidal product
⊗ in KL(D≤ ), but also about the operation ⊕, which plays a fundamental role in many
probabilistic frameworks [67, 19, 51]. As discussed in Example 13, the presence of ⊕ provides
a natural way of modelling probabilistic control and, perhaps more importantly, leads to a
structurally transparent axiomatisation. In addition to the equalities induced by the tape
construction in Figure 4, our axiomatisation comprises the three additional laws shown in
Figure 5. The third of these is an implication expressing cancellativity. Although not purely
equational, cancellativity is a standard reasoning principle that arises naturally in a wide
variety of algebraic structures.
    Relying on completeness for partial Boolean circuits and on a result from [7]–stated here
as Corollary 18–characterising tape diagrams as stochastic matrices of string diagrams, we
prove completeness for probabilistic Boolean tapes in Corollary 29. Consequently, as stated
in Corollary 30, semantic equality of probabilistic Boolean circuits reduces to equality of
their encodings as tapes.

Related Work. Figures 4 and 5 of [60] provide an axiomatisation of probabilistic Boolean
circuits. Crucially, the induced equivalence is strictly coarser than semantic equality, i.e.,
the one induced by ⟨⟨−⟩⟩. In fact, two diagrams c and d are equivalent in [60] if and only if
⟨⟨c⟩⟩ ∝ ⟨⟨d⟩⟩, where ∝ is the relation on KL(D≤ ) defined by f ∝ g whenever there exists λ > 0

 8       Conclusions and Future Work
We introduced an axiomatisation of partial Boolean circuits (Figures 1 and 3) and proved it
complete (Theorem 9). Extending this, we gave laws of probabilistic Boolean tapes (Figures 4
and 5) and, using a general result from [7], established their completeness (Corollary 29).
Combined with the encoding in [9], this allows checking semantic equality of probabilistic
Boolean circuits [60] (Corollary 30).
    In Example 13, it is shown that the combined use of ⊕ and ⊗ allows probabilistic tapes
to realise probabilistic control effectively. Extending tapes with traces for ⊕–following the
approach of [10], which provides a unifying account of several program logics [42, 56, 2, 24]–
would enable the representation of iteration and, potentially, provide algebraic foundations
for probabilistic program logics [48, 57]. Indeed, such extended tapes can encode probabilistic
